Using a shift-share instrumental variable approach that exploits peers’ flood exposure, we find that a $1,000 increase in flood insurance claims per single-family housing unit in the census-tract boosts housing prices by 1.38% after Hurricane Harvey in Houston, roughly $3,197 based on average housing values. While the median homeowner in flooded neighborhoods sees a 1.9% price decline after flooding, households in neighborhoods at the 75th percentile of flood insurance claims experience no such decrease. Moreover, homes that are less likely to be insured benefit from positive spillover effects and disadvantaged neighborhoods experience greater benefits from flood insurance claims. We also find suggestive evidence that well-insured tracts have fewer foreclosed properties and more home renovation. The increase in capitalized housing values represents approximately 50% of the total amount paid out in Harvey-related claims by the National Flood Insurance Program (FEMA).

title: CLIP-PING: Lightweight CLIP Models with Proximus Intrinsic Neighbors Guidance for Resource-Constrained Vision-Language Systems
affiliations: Kyung Hee University - Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyung Hee University - Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyung Hee University - Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyung Hee University and Kyung Hee University - Department of Computer Science and Engineering

detail.title: CLIP-PING: Lightweight CLIP Models with Proximus Intrinsic Neighbors Guidance for Resource-Constrained Vision-Language Systems
detail.abstract: Beyond the success of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), recent trends have increasingly marked a shift toward lightweight vision-language models for resource-constrained systems. However, such models often exhibit suboptimal performance when relying solely on a single image-text contrastive objective, spotlighting the need for more effective training mechanisms that guarantee robust cross-modal feature alignment. In this work, we propose CLIP-PING: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training with Proximus Intrinsic Neighbors Guidance, a novel yet simple and efficient training paradigm designed to improve the performance of lightweight vision-language models with minimal computational overhead and lower data demands. Specifically, CLIP-PING bootstraps unimodal features extracted from arbitrary pre-trained encoders to leverage intrinsic guidance of proximus neighbor samples, i.e., nearest-neighbors (NN) and cross nearest-neighbors (XNN). We find that the additional contrastive supervision induced by these neighbors substantially strengthens cross-modal alignment, enabling lightweight models to learn more generic features with enriched semantic diversity. Extensive experiments reveal that CLIP-PING notably surpasses its peers in zero-shot generalization and cross-modal retrieval tasks. In particular, a 5.5% improvement on zero-shot ImageNet1K classification, along with gains of 10.7% image-to-text (I2T) and 5.7% text-to-image (T2I) on Flickr30K retrieval, compared to the original CLIP when using ViT-XS image encoder trained on 3 million (image, text) pairs. Moreover, CLIP-PING showcases strong downstream transferability under the linear evaluation protocol across multiple image classification benchmarks.

title: Bioleaching of critical raw materials from bauxite residue with Aspergillus sp
affiliations: Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, University of Applied Sciences and Arts Northwestern Switzerland, Budapest University of Technology and Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bioleaching of critical raw materials from bauxite residue with Aspergillus sp
detail.abstract: Bauxite residue (red mud) represents a promising secondary resource for critical raw materials (CRMs). Biohydrometallurgy offers a potentially more sustainable alternative to conventional hydro- and pyrometallurgical routes for CRM recovery. In this study, an Aspergillus sp. was used to bioleach CRMs from bauxite residue (BR) under energy-efficient conditions, including a relatively low temperature (22 °C), a short contact time (5 days), and high pulp densities (up to 20 w/w%). During one-step bioleaching, fungal activity lowered the pH to 3.7‐4.8, depending on the BR concentration. The highest recovery efficiencies were achieved at 1% BR, reaching 77% Al, 47% Ti, 50% V, 42% Ga, 61% Y, 65% Zr, 20% La, 18% Ce, and 35% Nd. Increasing the BR concentration led to higher CRM concentrations in the leachate but reduced overall recovery efficiency. Vanadium extraction was maximised at 20 w/w% BR, yielding 48 mg/L in the leachate, corresponding to an 18% leaching efficiency. Ecotoxicological assessment revealed increased toxicity of the leaching residue obtained at 20% BR compared with the original material. Washing further increased residue toxicity and generated a toxic washing effluent, indicating that alternative post-treatment strategies are required. Overall, the results demonstrate that low-temperature, short-term fungal bioleaching at lower pulp densities can provide an environmentally favourable approach for CRM recovery from bauxite residue.

title: Modeling Trust in Central Bank Communication under Uncertainty: A Machine Learning–Driven Fractal Fuzzy Decision Support Mechanism
affiliations: Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul Medipol University, Istanbul Medipol University and Istanbul Medipol University

detail.title: Modeling Trust in Central Bank Communication under Uncertainty: A Machine Learning–Driven Fractal Fuzzy Decision Support Mechanism
detail.abstract: This study focuses on prioritizing strategies to enhance the impact of central bank communication policies on market confidence. The fundamental problem in this area is that, despite communication playing a critical role in monetary policy effectiveness and confidence building, it has not been clearly defined which communication dimensions and strategies should be prioritized. The current literature mostly emphasizes the general importance of communication, but studies that comparatively and quantitatively analyze the relative effects of different communication strategies are quite limited. The aim of this study is to identify the most prioritized criteria and strategies to strengthen the impact of central bank communication policy on market confidence and to analyze this process within the framework of a holistic decision-making model supported by artificial intelligence. To this end, a unique multi-criteria decision-making model based on Koch Snowflake fuzzy sets is proposed. In the model, 12 criteria and 6 communication strategies, determined through a literature review, are evaluated based on the opinions of 10 experts. The importance weights of the experts were calculated using machine learning techniques, and the criterion weights were calculated using the SIWEC method; the RATGOS approach was used to rank the strategies. The robustness of the results was tested using RAM and MUNRA methods. The findings indicate that the contribution to the perception of political independence and the clarity of forward guidance are the most influential criteria for trust.

title: Do shifts in green energy fund flows affect financial markets and economic growth?
affiliations: University of Sussex, Bank of Japan and Vlerick Business School

detail.title: Do shifts in green energy fund flows affect financial markets and economic growth?
detail.abstract: Why has financing related to green energy funds progressed more slowly than needed to address climate concerns, and does accelerating this transition risk undermining financial markets or economic growth? Using data on US green and brown energy funds, we examine the dynamics of capital reallocation between these two segments. We find a time-varying shift from brown to green energy investments, largely influenced by policy-driven climate news rather than long-term temperature trends. The speed of this reallocation is closely linked to changes in US climate policy. Moreover, while climate news shocks tend to depress stock returns and industrial production, these effects are significantly moderated by the presence of green energy funds, which act as a stabilizing buffer. Overall, our findings suggest that accelerated green energy fund flows can enhance both financial stability and real economic performance.

title: Environmental Pressure Measurement: A Composite and Discriminant Approach
affiliations: University of Genoa, University of Genoa and University of Genoa

detail.title: Environmental Pressure Measurement: A Composite and Discriminant Approach
detail.abstract: This paper presents a planning-focused statistical approach to the measurement and interpretation of environmental pressure in diverse economic systems. The paper concentrates on OECD and BRICS nations during the period 2000-2023, using a distance-based composite indicator and multivariate classification methods to inform evidence-based environmental and industrial planning. Environmental pressure is assessed by a non-compensatory composite index based on carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrate emissions, reflecting structural stress generated by energy consumption, industry, and agriculture. The composite index facilitates longitudinal analysis and cross-national comparison, offering a composite yet policy-useful measure of aggregate environmental pressure. To provide a dynamic perspective, Linear Discriminant Analysis is used to assess whether emission structures distinguish statistically advanced and emerging economies and to specify transition or hybrid patterns. The findings indicate the persistent diversity of institutional categories and the increasingly blurred line between OECD and BRICS nations. Misclassifications are interpreted not as model errors, but as statistically meaningful signals of structural transition and partial convergence in emission profiles. This evidence challenges rigid development-based classifications and supports a continuum-based interpretation of environmental pressure. From a socio-economic planning perspective, the proposed framework enhances statistical measurement for sustainability by linking composite indicators with structural diagnostics. It provides a decision-support tool for identifying transition cases, monitoring convergence processes, and designing differentiated environmental policies aligned with country-specific emission structures rather than institutional labels alone.

title: The Impact of Global PV Solar Expansion on Gold and Silver Price Dynamics: Machine Learning Forecasts and Economic Implications
affiliations: Universitas Halu Oleo

detail.title: The Impact of Global PV Solar Expansion on Gold and Silver Price Dynamics: Machine Learning Forecasts and Economic Implications
detail.abstract: This study investigates how global photovoltaic (PV) solar expansion shapes gold and silver price dynamics using a novel annual dataset (2000–2024) and a hybrid empirical framework. The analysis integrates standard econometric tools (ADF, Johansen cointegration, panel OLS, Granger causality) with machine learning forecasts (LSTM and XGBoost), interpretability (SHAP), and stress testing to capture both causal channels and predictive performance. The results revealed three main findings. First, the Granger causality tests indicate that cumulative PV capacity significantly influences gold prices at short lags (1–2), while the effect on silver is statistically insignificant, pointing to indirect channels through macroeconomic factors and portfolio rebalancing. Second, panel regressions show that PV-driven silver demand exerts a modest impact on silver prices, whereas macroeconomic factors (the USD index, inflation, and geopolitical risk) remain the dominant drivers for both metals. Third, XGBoost provides superior out-of-sample accuracy compared to LSTM, and SHAP analysis highlights a multi-year lag structure (approximately four years) for the PV capacity effects. Stress testing further indicates that precious metals remain highly sensitive to macro shocks despite structural pressures from PV expansion. This study contributes a unified dataset, documents a causality paradox between PV expansion and precious metals, and demonstrates the practical value of combining machine learning with econometric methods for scenario forecasting. The policy implications include the need for strategic mineral planning, dynamic hedging strategies, and central bank awareness of energy-transition effects on inflation expectations.

title: Robust Firm-Level Revenue Forecasting Using Stacked Hybrid Ensemble Frameworks:Evidence from the Semiconductor Industry
affiliations: National Taipei University of Technology, National Taipei University of Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Robust Firm-Level Revenue Forecasting Using Stacked Hybrid Ensemble Frameworks:Evidence from the Semiconductor Industry
detail.abstract: Accurate revenue forecasting is essential for financial planning, resource allocation, and strategic decision-making in the volatile semiconductor industry. This study proposes the Stacked Hybrid Ensemble (SHE) framework, a novel forecasting architecture that integrates long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, Transformer models, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) to predict monthly revenue for Taiwan-listed semiconductor firms. Our approach incorporates time series decomposition to analyze trend, seasonality, and residual components, and examines how firm size impacts forecast accuracy. The proposed SHE framework combines stacking ensemble with a dynamic weighting mechanism to adaptively fuse model predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that SHE outperforms all individual models across four error metrics, achieving up to a 35.4% improvement in mean squared error (MSE). Through rigorous statistical validation using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, we confirm that SHE’s performance superiority is systematic and statistically significant (p =1.49×10−8) across all 26 companies, providing high reliability for practical applications. For business practitioners and investors, these findings offer substantial value: (1) financial managers can enhance budgeting accuracy and cash-flow planning; (2) operations directors can improve production scheduling and inventory management; and (3) investors gain more reliable tools for company valuation and risk assessment. The framework’s consistent performance across different firm sizes makes it particularly valuable for portfolio analysis and supply-chain decision-making in the cyclical semiconductor sector.

title: The introduction of Japan-made banknotes into Taiwan during Japanese Occupation Time（1895-1945）
affiliations: Wuhan Business University and Kansai University

detail.title: The introduction of Japan-made banknotes into Taiwan during Japanese Occupation Time（1895-1945）
detail.abstract: This study examines the introduction and circulation of Japan-made banknotes in colonial Taiwan during the early years of Japanese rule (1899-1905). Following the establishment of the Bank of Taiwan in 1899, the Japanese government sought to modernize Taiwan's chaotic monetary system through paper currency. Drawing upon primary sources including Taiwan Daily News reports and official Bank of Taiwan documents, we trace banknote design adaptation, printing procedures, transportation logistics, and circulation promotion. Our analysis reveals that banknote circulation expanded from 2,276,411 yen (September 1900) to 6,214,372 yen (September 1905), representing a 173% increase. By 1901, Taiwan Banknotes constituted 59.7% of all currency in circulation. Regional analysis shows significant geographic variation, with Taichung exhibiting the most dramatic increase (from 2.9% to 92.1% between January 1900 and May 1901). These findings illuminate colonial monetary policy implementation and economic integration between Taiwan and Japan.

title: Cross-sectoral and spatial impacts of carbon neutrality on China's transport sector emissions: A 31-region CGE analysis
affiliations: China Electric Power Research Institute, Nankai University, Peking University, China Electric Power Research Institute, Tianjin University, Nankai University and Peking University

detail.title: Cross-sectoral and spatial impacts of carbon neutrality on China's transport sector emissions: A 31-region CGE analysis
detail.abstract: The carbon peaking and carbon neutrality strategy is reshaping China’s industrial structure, with profound yet underexplored ripple effects on the transportation industry—a key pillar of the national economy. From the perspective of the industrial chain and regional correlation, this study employs a Computable General Equilibrium (IMED|CGE) model covering 31 Chinese provinces to assess how upstream industrial changes under carbon neutrality policies cascade into the transport sector’s scale, output, and emissions. Combining structural path decomposition, we trace the industrial and spatial pathways through which emission reductions propagate. Findings reveal that carbon neutrality policies trigger systemic shifts in transport demand by restructuring industries and reduce its CO2 emissions by 43.1% in 2060. The policy-induced contraction of energy-intensive sectors, such as coal and steel, leads to a sharp decline in transport inputs for these industries (e.g., by $26.9 billion and $28.3 billion, respectively), directly curtailing high-carbon bulk freight. Conversely, the expansion of low-carbon services stimulates a significant increase in transport demand (by $87.0 billion), fostering a structural shift towards high-value, lower-emission freight. Meanwhile, transport electrification and efficiency gains amplify these effects. Spatially, impacts vary significantly. The transportation sector in energy-exporting provinces (e.g., Shanxi, Inner Mongolia) achieves the most significant emission reductions (up to 78.4%), with core reduction pathways primarily concentrated in upstream production processes (e.g., coal mining). In economically diversified regions (e.g., Guangdong, Chongqing), cuts occur more in downstream consumption, such as reduced transport linked to local construction and services. We recommend that energy-exporting regions prioritize upstream green supply development, while economically advanced areas focus on downstream low-carbon consumption. Synergizing “upstream green supply” with “downstream low-carbon consumption” can drive a comprehensive green transition across China’s transport sector.

title: A novel online deep learning regression controller for effective real-time maximum demand reductions using battery energy storage system
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tunku Abdul Rahman University (UTAR) - Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A novel online deep learning regression controller for effective real-time maximum demand reductions using battery energy storage system
detail.abstract: Maximum demand (MD) is the highest peak demand of all the daily peak demands over a month. Battery energy storage system (BESS) can be used and controlled appropriately to reduce the monthly maximum demands such that customers can reduce their maximum demand charges and power utility companies can defer their network reinforcement and augmentation of generating capacity. It is important to ensure that any technique employed for BESS to reduce MD is consistent and reliable in reducing every single daily peak demand to deliver the financial benefits. An online deep learning regression controller is a new control technique introduced in this paper that is different from conventional methods. This technique operates using its regression ability to generate the best possible threshold in real-time such that BESS supplies real power to the load when the load demand exceeds the threshold. This regression ability is absent in the published BESS controllers. Its regression ability is trained with the historical data and actively updated with its new data by using its online learning feature to capture any long-term changes in the demand due to the human behavioural or climate changes. The performance of the controller is evaluated through simulation and real-world experiment. The simulation studies show that the controller achieves improved performance when benchmarked against other deep learning models and existing controllers with an average maximum demand reduction factor of 75.08%. The DLR controller achieves about 10.89% higher maximum demand reduction than the next closest contender. Furthermore, the experimental results validate its effectiveness, showing an average maximum demand reduction factor of 73.49%. Overall, the online proposed controller effectively reduces maximum demands in both simulation and real-world scenarios, achieving an improvement of 175.42% compared to a battery system with basic scheduling.

title: Beyond arbitrage: How PUE-linked electricity pricing reshapes the selection of data center waste heat recovery strategies
affiliations: Tianjin University, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangdong University of Technology, Tianjin University, Tianjin University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tianjin University and Tianjin University

detail.title: Beyond arbitrage: How PUE-linked electricity pricing reshapes the selection of data center waste heat recovery strategies
detail.abstract: With the rapid development of data centers, efficient waste heat recovery from cooling systems has become increasingly important for energy conservation and carbon reduction. However, under electricity pricing policies linked to Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), the thermo-economic performance of waste heat recovery systems is fundamentally reshaped, yet remains insufficiently investigated. Against this background, this study examines representative waste heat recovery systems for data centers. Theoretical limits in terms of maximum PUE reduction and power generation profit are first derived, followed by thermodynamic and thermo-economic analyses with PUE-linked penalty pricing explicitly incorporated to quantify the actual energy-saving effects and their influence on the recovery system selection. Finally, Shanghai is adopted as a case study to evaluate the full-year operational performance of different recovery schemes under penalty pricing constraints. Results demonstrate that recovery schemes prioritizing PUE reduction to eliminate penalty costs are superior: in Shanghai, the resulting operating cost savings are nearly three times the power generation profit, with annual cost reduced by up to 27.11% under organic Rankine cycle operation. For newly built data centers, integrating thermal storage at design stage enables simultaneous reductions in PUE and Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE). Overall, this work provides a region-adaptive perspective and practical decision support for selecting waste heat recovery strategies under diverse regional conditions.

title: PaSTNet: A Multimodal Model for High-resolution Parking Search Time Estimates
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: PaSTNet: A Multimodal Model for High-resolution Parking Search Time Estimates
detail.abstract: Evaluating parking difficulty is critical for urban planning and policy, including parking pricing, demand management, parking facility allocation, and curb space regulation. Reliable estimates of parking difficulty are also essential for commercial applications such as routing and navigation systems. However, accurately estimating parking difficulty at large scale remains challenging for several reasons. First, large-scale parking data are difficult to collect or are commercially restricted. Uncovering parking patterns requires extensive historical data with rich spatial and temporal coverage. Second, parking behavior exhibits substantial spatial heterogeneity due to the combined effects of road characteristics and the surrounding built environment. In this paper, we quantify parking difficulty with parking search time (PST) and propose a multimodal framework - PaSTNet - for estimating PST for each road segment at city scale. PaSTNet integrates a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to capture spatial dependencies in parking behavior. Visual features reflecting curbside and roadway conditions are extracted from satellite imagery using a large-scale pre-trained visual foundation model DINO-v2. A cross-attention module is then employed to fuse visual embeddings with trajectory-based features and road characteristics, enabling the model to jointly learn from network structure and visual context. Experimental results demonstrate that PaSTNet consistently outperforms baseline methods. In addition, this study provides insights into the spatiotemporal distribution of parking difficulty across urban areas.

title: Determinants of Women’s Participation in Leadership and Management of Agricultural Cooperatives in Endamohoni, Tigray, Ethiopia
affiliations: Humera Agricultural Research Center - Tigray Agricultural Research Institute, Mekelle University and The Australian National University

detail.title: Determinants of Women’s Participation in Leadership and Management of Agricultural Cooperatives in Endamohoni, Tigray, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: AbstractWomen's participation in all economic, social, and political spheres is crucial for a country’s development. In most developing countries, such as Ethiopia, women’s participation in various managerial activities is low, particularly in leadership and decision-making. The objectives of the study were to assess the governance structure of agricultural cooperatives, examine the extent of participation of women members in leadership positions, and identify the factors that affect women’s participation in agricultural cooperative leadership. A multi-stage sampling procedure was followed for the selection of sample women members.  Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and an ordered logit regression model. The participation of women in each leadership position should ideally be 50% or a minimum of 30%. However, for the study cooperatives, it was 11.11%. 40% women never participated in the main cooperative activities. Findings from the ordered logistics show that age, experience and education level of the household head and the household’s family size, non-farm income earning, livestock endowment, farm land endowment, and home distance to cooperative were found to be the determinant factors that affect the level of women’s participation in management and leadership of cooperatives.

title: Lipschitz-Regularized Path-Strength Refactoring for Differentiable Architecture Search
affiliations: Jinan University, Jinan University, Jinan University and Jinan University

detail.title: Lipschitz-Regularized Path-Strength Refactoring for Differentiable Architecture Search
detail.abstract: Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) has significantly advanced neural architecture search through efficient gradient-based optimization, yet it remains hindered by optimization instability and the notorious “performance collapse” issue. In this paper, we propose Lip-DARTS, a novel framework that addresses these challenges via Lipschitz-regularized search space reformulation and path-strength refactoring. By imposing strict Lipschitz constraints, we stabilize the gradient landscape and establish a rigorous connection between loss functions and path gradients. This theoretical foundation enables the decoupling of the traditionally unstable bi-level optimization into a sequential single-level process. Specifically, architecture selection is refactored into the evaluation of path-strength metrics, allowing the search to be efficiently conducted via heuristic optimization algorithms such as Simulated Annealing (SA). Experimental results and ablation studies demonstrate that Lip-DARTS not only maintains high efficiency but also effectively circumvents performance collapse, particularly the over-representation of skip connections. Specifically, it achieves a test error of 3.11% on CIFAR-10 and an error rate of 18.74% on CIFAR-100. Notably, the method reduces the marginal search cost to merely 0.04 GPU days, offering a stable and practitioner-friendly solution for discovering high-performance architectures across diverse datasets.

title: The future generation of lightweight materials? A Life Cycle Assessment of fiber-reinforced composite cross car beams
affiliations: RWTH Aachen University, RWTH Aachen University, RWTH Aachen University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Dresden University of Technology, Dresden University of Technology, Dresden University of Technology and Dresden University of Technology

detail.title: The future generation of lightweight materials? A Life Cycle Assessment of fiber-reinforced composite cross car beams
detail.abstract: Fiber-reinforced composites offer promising lightweight alternatives for automotive applications, yet comprehensive life cycle assessments (LCAs) comparing them with conventional metal components remain limited. This study presents the first cradle-to-grave LCA evaluating a recyclable multi-material glass-fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) composite cross car beam (CCB) against an aluminium reference, considering 11 CML midpoint impact categories under different scenarios. The study has been conducted as part of a larger research project aimed at supporting the development of a more sustainable GFRP composite CCB. The composite redesign achieves lower cradle-to-grave impacts across 10 of 11 categories, with reductions of 35–37% in toxicity-related impact categories and 8–16% in Global Warming Potential. Ozone Depletion Potential represents the only trade-off (~12–13% increase), attributable to proxy-based inventory data. Despite replacing ~40% of the aluminium mass, residual aluminium supply for the hybrid composite structure dominates upstream impacts, while end-of-life (EoL) recycling credits prove decisive for resource depletion categories. These results indicate that environmental performance in hybrid multi-material composite architectures is governed by metal substitution, scrap minimization, and EoL recycling quality - conditions increasingly decisive as powertrains electrify and electricity grids decarbonize.

title: Percepta: A perception-driven world-model for agent-based simulation and social system modeling
affiliations: Guangzhou City University of Technology

detail.title: Percepta: A perception-driven world-model for agent-based simulation and social system modeling
detail.abstract: Percepta is a perception-driven world-model simulation framework for agent-based modeling of social and economic systems under evolving macro conditions and institutional rules. The software formalizes perception as an explicit computational layer and adopts a world-first architecture in which global state representation and state transitions are modeled independently of agent heuristics. This design enables controlled experimentation on how heterogeneous agents form subjective interpretations and how collective outcomes emerge from their interaction with a dynamically evolving environment. Implemented in Python, Percepta integrates a simulation engine, modular world and agent components, persistent data storage, and a web-based interface for interactive exploration. The framework is domain-agnostic and supports reproducible simulation studies in policy analysis and computational social science.

title: Immigrants Use ChatGPT More and Differently: Nativity, Duration of Stay, and Primary Language Differences in First- and Second-Level Adoption
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Immigrants Use ChatGPT More and Differently: Nativity, Duration of Stay, and Primary Language Differences in First- and Second-Level Adoption
detail.abstract: A growing body of research has documented demographic disparities in generative AI adoption by age, education, income, and race/ethnicity, but whether adoption differs by immigration status remains unknown. Using data from the Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (N=9,151), this study applied Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition to estimate the nativity gap in first-level AI adoption (ChatGPT awareness, ChatGPT ever use) and second-level AI adoption (specific use cases of entertainment, learning, and work tasks), and to determine how much of any observed difference is attributable to group characteristics versus differences in how those characteristics relate to outcomes. Findings show that foreign-born adults had higher rates of ChatGPT awareness (77.0% vs. 69.4%) and ChatGPT use (43.4% vs. 32.7%) after adjusting for age and gender. Among ChatGPT users, foreign-born adults were significantly more likely to use ChatGPT for learning (34.9% vs. 22.5%, p < .001). Age, education, race/ethnicity, and digital access were the primary contributors to the explained gap, though the relative importance of each factor varied across outcomes. For first-level adoption (ChatGPT awareness), sociodemographic differences accounted for 63% of the 9.9 percentage-point gap, with a significant unexplained component remaining (3.6 pp, adjusted p = .013) after FDR correction. For second-level adoption (ChatGPT use for learning), race/ethnicity alone accounted for nearly 80% of the explained gap. Recent immigrants (0-10 years in the U.S.) showed the highest ChatGPT engagement at the second level of adoption, and Spanish-language respondents reported lower first-level adoption of awareness (58.9% vs. 70.7%, p < .001) after adjusting for age and gender. These findings indicate that immigrant disadvantage in technology adoption does not extend to ChatGPT, and that language access and purpose of use are additional dimensions of AI inequality beyond nativity alone.

title: When place matters more: How state ownership amplifies local institutional effects on firms’ productive assets
affiliations: SKEMA Business School, Université Côte d'Azur (GREDEG), Luiss Guido Carli University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When place matters more: How state ownership amplifies local institutional effects on firms’ productive assets
detail.abstract: Governments deploy state-owned enterprises (SOEs) as policy instruments to support regional productive capacity, yet whether this instrument is equally effective across local institutional contexts within developed economies remains unclear. Using panel data for 47,978 Italian firms (2007–2015) matched to province-level institutional quality measures, we examine whether local institutional quality conditions SOEs’ ability to sustain tangible fixed-asset stocks relative to privately owned enterprises (POEs). We find that local institutional quality significantly shapes firms’ fixed-asset stocks, even within a developed economy. Contrary to expectations, SOEs’ fixed assets are more sensitive than POEs’ ones to higher local institutional quality, especially among smaller SOEs. Results are robust to instrumental variable estimation using 19th-century provincial indicators. These findings reveal a paradox: SOE-based regional development policies are conditional on local institutional quality, i.e., the instrument underperforms precisely in weak-institution provinces where policy support is most needed.

title: Coevolution or Co-Movement? Dynamic Linkages between Material Footprint and Environmental Taxation in the EU’s Net-Zero Transition
affiliations: University of Reading - Henley Business School, and University of Reading - Henley Business School

detail.title: Coevolution or Co-Movement? Dynamic Linkages between Material Footprint and Environmental Taxation in the EU’s Net-Zero Transition
detail.abstract: Achieving net‑zero requires understanding how policy instruments and resource‑use trajectories jointly evolve, yet the dynamic relationship between environmental taxation and material intensity remains underexplored. This paper examines whether environmental taxation and the material footprint coevolve across EU member states during the net‑zero transition. Drawing on transition theory and a co‑evolutionary perspective, we analyse a balanced panel of 19 EU countries (2007–2023) using a design‑sensitive empirical strategy that combines dynamic fixed‑effects models, Dumitrescu–Hurlin Granger tests, PDOLS, PMG‑ARDL estimators, and system‑level diagnostics. Across estimators, environmental tax intensity exhibits a robust negative long‑run association with MF, while short‑run responses are limited, consistent with socio‑technical change unfolding through gradual, path‑dependent adjustments rather than immediate reactions. We also find short‑run bidirectional linkages, indicating that shifts in material use can prompt fiscal recalibration even as taxes ultimately lead long‑run adjustment. These findings position environmental taxation as a directional lever whose effects strengthen when situated within broader circular‑economy policy architectures. More broadly, the study demonstrates how co‑evolutionary analytical approaches can clarify the temporal dynamics through which policy mixes shape structural decoupling in accelerating net‑zero transitions.

title: From Vertical Integration to Horizontal Architectures: Reciprocation Points, Hybridization, and Dominant Designs in Telecom (1980–2010)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, ZHAW School of Management and Law, University of Tartu and University of Helsinki - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: From Vertical Integration to Horizontal Architectures: Reciprocation Points, Hybridization, and Dominant Designs in Telecom (1980–2010)
detail.abstract: How do incumbents adapt to technological discontinuities while remaining anchored in path-dependent assets and routines? Prior research explains industry evolution through the discontinuity–ferment–dominant design sequence and models innovation as an inverted-U function of cognitive distance, but these perspectives are rarely integrated. In our study from vertical integration to horizontal architecture, we adopt an industry‑architecture lens that clarifies how shifts in interfaces, standards, and layers reorganize value capture and capability deployment. Within this lens, we theorize the reciprocation point and its management— the short window between technological discontinuity and dominant‑design selection—where incumbents can simultaneously extend legacy paths and create new ones. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Telecom Finland/Sonera (1980–2010), we show that the dynamically optimal cognitive distance between incumbents and learning partners shifts across the industry life cycle: higher during ferment and lower after dominant-design stabilization. Our study contributes to theory in three ways: First, we extend interactive learning theory by specifying a dynamic stage-contingent optimum within the discontinuity–ferment–dominant design cycle. Second, we demonstrate how path-dependent asset structures and attention mechanisms condition feasible learning distances and shape the timing of reciprocation. Third, by integrating demand-side preference overlapping with cognitive distance, we clarify when hybrids generate value under architectural transition and how horizontalization reshapes appropriability.

title: The Health and Economic Costs of Welfare Reform: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of the Roll-out of Universal Credit in England
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Department of Economics, The University of Manchester - School of Health Sciences, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems, Newcastle University - Population Health Sciences Institute, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems, University of Glasgow - MRC/CSO Social and Public Health Sciences Unit, Newcastle University, Northumbria University, University of Glasgow - Institute of Health and Wellbeing, University of Glasgow - Institute of Health and Wellbeing, University of Liverpool, Newcastle University, University of Essex, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems and The University of Manchester

detail.title: The Health and Economic Costs of Welfare Reform: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of the Roll-out of Universal Credit in England
detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on the mental health and healthcare utilisation impacts of the roll-out of Universal Credit, one of the most significant welfare reforms in Europe in recent decades. Designed to simplify the benefit system and strengthen work incentives by merging six means-tested programmes into a single payment, Universal Credit also introduced features that may adversely affect mental health. Exploiting the plausibly exogenous, staggered geographical introduction of Universal Credit across England between 2013 and 2018, we implement a staggered difference-in-differences design using comprehensive small-area administrative data on clinically recorded mental health and related healthcare utilisation. We find substantial adverse effects of Universal Credit exposure: a 0.10 standard-deviation increase in clinically diagnosed depression prevalence, a 0.03 standard-deviation increase in mental health-related hospital admissions and attendances, and a 0.06 standard-deviation rise in antidepressant prescribing. In natural units, these correspond to approximately 113,742 additional cases of diagnosed depression, 29,993 extra hospital admissions and attendances, and 1.29 million additional antidepressant prescriptions annually by 2018. Results are robust across specifications, sensitivity analyses, spatial aggregation, and alternative estimators. Because outcomes are measured at the small-area level, our estimates capture population-wide effects that combine direct impacts on Universal Credit recipients with spillovers to non-recipients. Indicative valuations imply sizeable associated quality-of-life losses and direct healthcare costs of approximately £2.84 billion per year. These findings highlight that welfare reforms can generate substantial mental health externalities and underscore the importance of incorporating health and healthcare system consequences into social policy design and evaluation.

title: How Banking Regulation Affects Collusion Sustainability: A Multimarket Contact Approach
affiliations: Universidade do Porto - Faculdade de Economia (FEP), NOVA University Lisbon and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Banking Regulation Affects Collusion Sustainability: A Multimarket Contact Approach
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how regulatory instruments affect collusion sustainability in banking within a theoretical framework where: (i) banks compete simultaneously in loan and deposit markets characterized by different degrees of product differentiation; (ii) strategic interaction occurs through an infinitely repeated game with Nash reversion strategies; and (iii) capital requirements, reserve ratios, and interbank rates alter the relative profitability of each market. We show that the impact of these instruments on collusion depends critically on relative market differentiation: the same regulatory instrument can either facilitate or hinder coordination depending on which market exhibits greater product homogeneity. This non-monotonicity implies that regulators must account for market structure when calibrating policy instruments to avoid unintended effects on competitive intensity.

title: CMIE: Channel Merging Before Independent Embedding in Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Technology, Zhejiang University of Technology, Zhejiang University of Technology, Zhejiang University of Technology, Zhejiang University of Technology and Zhejiang University of Technology

detail.title: CMIE: Channel Merging Before Independent Embedding in Time Series Forecasting
detail.abstract: Time-series data are widely present across various domains, including climate, finance, and healthcare. Accurate time series forecasting can uncover trends and patterns within such data, offering forward-looking insights to support decision-making in these fields. In recent years, the channel-independence  strategy has been proposed, and it has been observed that this strategy, which ignores inter-channel dependencies. However, inter-channel correlations are clearly one of the essential features in multivariate time-series data, and neglecting them can limit the model's predictive capability. Therefore, we propose a Channel-wise data merging and Independent Embedding framework, named “CMIE”. Specifically, we design a data merging method that captures the temporal dependencies across different channels, along with a channel-independent embedding method that encodes each channel separately. This approach not only fully considers the inter-channel correlations but also enhances model robustness through the CI strategy, achieving strong forecasting performance while reducing the risk of overfitting. Specifically, we adopt a channel-independent  approach, treating each channel as an independent variable, constructing individual prompts for each channel, and aggregating them to independently guide the time series forecasting. We evaluate “CMIE” on multiple long-horizon forecasting datasets with correlated channels, and the results demonstrate that “CMIE” significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art time-series forecasting methods.

title: Do Delayed Nursing Home Admissions Increase Hospitalisations and Costs?
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management, University of York, University of York - Centre for Health Economics, University of York - Department of Economics and Related Studies and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management

detail.title: Do Delayed Nursing Home Admissions Increase Hospitalisations and Costs?
detail.abstract: We study the effects of delayed nursing home admissions on urgent hospitalisations and costs in the Netherlands. We exploit plausibly exogenous variation in within-region congestion for nursing home admissions. A one-month delay increases urgent hospitalisation by 2.6 percentage points (15% of the baseline), mostly due to falls and primarily driven by individuals with dementia living alone. Cost savings in nursing home care due to delays are partly offset by increased costs in home care and hospitals. These findings suggest that timely access and improved allocation of scarce nursing home capacity can yield health benefits and reduce costs in other parts of the healthcare sector.

title: Do Media Awards Shift Retention Incentives? Evidence from CEO Turnover
affiliations: University of Reading - Henley Business School,, University of Durham, Glasgow University and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Do Media Awards Shift Retention Incentives? Evidence from CEO Turnover
detail.abstract: Drawing on career concerns theory, this study examines how media-conferred CEO awards affect CEO turnover. Using a matched difference-in-differences design and a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2005 to 2023, we find that CEO turnover increases significantly following award receipt. This effect is accompanied by greater managerial visibility, increased external engagement, and stronger internal scrutiny, and is weaker when CEOs face stronger incentives to remain in office, such as higher compensation growth potential or longer remaining career horizons. Post-turnover firm performance does not improve and stock returns decline, suggesting that award-induced CEO departures are unlikely to reflect improved governance. Overall, the results indicate that media recognition can generate unintended effects on executive retention.

title: Fales Hopes: The Impact of National Leaders' Firm Visits on Industry Peers
affiliations: University of Melbourne and University of Strathclyde - Strathclyde Business School

detail.title: Fales Hopes: The Impact of National Leaders' Firm Visits on Industry Peers
detail.abstract: We examine how politicians’ routine activities influence the corporate sector in the short and long run. Using hand-collected data on firm visits by China’s national leaders, we show that industry peers of visited firms experience a 1.5% value increase in the short-run, consistent with investors interpreting these visits as favorable industry-wide signals. In contrast, these firms exhibit significant performance declines of more than 15% over the subsequent three years. We provide evidence that peers increase R&D investment following visits in anticipation of government support, but on average receive insufficient resources to sustain these investments, resulting in overinvestment and poorer performance. The decline is attenuated for firms better positioned to secure government support, including state-owned firms, politically connected firms, and firms in provincially designated strategic industries. Overall, our findings highlight how political signaling can distort capital allocation by generating optimistic expectations without commensurate follow-through, leading to adverse long-run real effects.

title: Wealth Dynamics and Asset Prices with Heterogeneous Beliefs under Smooth Ambiguity
affiliations: The University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Wealth Dynamics and Asset Prices with Heterogeneous Beliefs under Smooth Ambiguity
detail.abstract: We study heterogeneous-agent economies with long-run risk and smooth ambiguity where the persistent component of aggregate consumption growth is unobservable. Agents holding different beliefs are averse to uncertainty arising from state estimation. By examining a two-agent model with an elasticity of intertemporal substitution above 1 and reasonable risk aversion, we find that ambiguity generates an uncertainty-sharing motive that leads to long-run survival of both agents while without ambiguity the agent holding correct beliefs dominate in the long run. In addition, time-varying welfare weights of agents and their posterior beliefs produce model-implied price-dividend ratios that can predict returns in the data.

title: Political Control Over Redistricting and the Partisan Balance in Congress∗
affiliations: , Towson University and Kenyon College

detail.title: Political Control Over Redistricting and the Partisan Balance in Congress∗
detail.abstract: We estimate the impact of a political party’s ability to unilaterally redistrict Congressional seats upon partisan seat share allocations in the U.S. House of Representatives. Controlling for stateXdecade and year effects, we find an 8.3 percentage point increase in the Republican House seat share in the three elections following Republican control over redistricting in the 2000 and 2010 redistricting cycles. We only find significant effects for Democrats in large states. Effects are one half of the average seat gap between the parties in the 2010s. Differences across parties reflect more denied trifectas due to an opposite party governor in Democratic states and greater impacts for Republicans in small states. Differences do not reflect a rise in racial gerrymandering.

title: The Effects of Education on Corruption: Evidence from Vietnam’s University Expansion
affiliations: Duke University - Department of Political Science, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics, Charles River Associates (CRA) and National University Singapore

detail.title: The Effects of Education on Corruption: Evidence from Vietnam’s University Expansion
detail.abstract: Education and corruption are negatively correlated at the cross-national level, but little is known about the causal relationship between the two. We combine newly-collected data on timing and locations of Vietnam’s national expansion of universities with detailed survey data on experiences of corruption from over 170,000 respondents in 320 districts across 12 years. Using staggered difference-in-differences, we show that cohorts exposed to the university expansion are 78% more likely to have a university education. However, this increase neither translates into fewer individuals being affected by corruption nor increases the propensity to denounce corrupt officials. Instead, we find that education increases exposure to corruption at the individual level. The mechanism for this increase that is most consistent with our data is that education raises household income and higher income leads to more bribe payments.

title: Crime and Prices: Evidence From Thefts of Expensive Precious Metal
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP), Singapore Management University and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Crime and Prices: Evidence From Thefts of Expensive Precious Metal
detail.abstract: We study whether economic incentives matter for crime in a novel way, through study of expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters. We combine sharp, plausibly exogenous variation in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters with newly assembled U.S. data and multiple research designs. We show that phenomenally fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable and rapid rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that both demand- and supply-side economic forces shape property crime and inform targeted deterrence policies.

title: ASSESSING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF PARTICIPATORY IRRIGATION MANAGEMENT IN EASTERN UGANDA: A case study of the Doho Irrigation Scheme
affiliations: Busitema University, Busitema University, Busitema University and Busitema University

detail.title: ASSESSING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF PARTICIPATORY IRRIGATION MANAGEMENT IN EASTERN UGANDA: A case study of the Doho Irrigation Scheme
detail.abstract: Participatory Irrigation Management (PIM) is widely promoted as a mechanism for improving irrigation performance, water conservation, and institutional sustainability in water-scarce regions. However, evidence on its operational effectiveness remains limited, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. This study assessed the effectiveness of PIM implementation at the Doho Irrigation Scheme in Eastern Uganda, with emphasis on policy implementation, institutional performance, farmer participation, and water management outcomes. Data were collected through structured questionnaires, focus group discussions, interviews, and field observations, and analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, regression modelling, and chi-square tests. Results indicate that PIM effectiveness was low, with only 12% of policies reported as fully effective, largely constrained by limited resources (32%) and low policy awareness (average awareness index = 0.28). Despite these challenges, strong positive relationships were observed between farmer participation and system outcomes. Farmer satisfaction showed a near-perfect correlation with future participation (r = 0.999), explaining 99.8% of the variation in participation levels (R² = 0.998). Participation in decision-making was significantly associated with higher agricultural output (χ² = 11.75), while PIM participation was positively correlated with adoption of water conservation practices (r = 0.7). However, farmer–institution interaction remained weak, with 40% of respondents reporting rare contact with PIM staff. The findings demonstrate that while PIM implementation remains limited, strengthening institutional capacity, improving farmer engagement, and increasing interaction frequency can substantially enhance irrigation performance and sustainability. These insights are relevant to irrigation schemes across developing and water-stressed regions globally.

title: Goldilocks literacy and IPO underpricing in Europe
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Goldilocks literacy and IPO underpricing in Europe
detail.abstract: This paper examines the non-linear relation between country-level financial and digital literacy of initial public offering (IPOs) underpricing in European stock markets. Analyzing 874 European IPOs from 2015-2024, using quadratic regression models with controls for offer size, firm age, overallotment provisions, foreign direct investment, month-of-issuance, and industry fixed effects, we identify a U-shaped pattern between IPOs underpricing and financial and digital literacy scores. Our results indicate that IPO underpricing is minimized at intermediate levels of financial literacy, therefore highlighting that countries with high and low financial literacy scores exhibit first-day returns that are higher than those observed for those with moderate financial literacy levels. For digital literacy (DL), we document a similar yet asymmetric U-shaped pattern peaking at a score of 65.1, within a range of 0-100. Moving from very low digital literacy (DL = 10) to this Goldilocks point reduces underpricing by 30 percentage points (pp). In contrast, increasing DL beyond this point, up to a score of 90, raises underpricing by only 7 pp.  The non-linear dual-literacy effects documented here extend prior linear models and highlight that human capital—specifically financial and digital skills—influences primary market pricing efficiency, with implications for issuers, underwriters, investors, and regulators seeking to optimize pricing design and market functioning. Overall, this study makes meaningful contributions to literature by extending behavioral IPO theory to incorporate (i) dual literacy and (ii) nonlinear effects that are absent from prior linear models.

title: Evaluation of a Hybridity Trap in the Payments for Forest Ecosystem Services program in North-West Vietnam
affiliations: Vietnam National University (VNU) - VNU University of Economics and Business, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Padua and The University of Sydney - School of Economics

detail.title: Evaluation of a Hybridity Trap in the Payments for Forest Ecosystem Services program in North-West Vietnam
detail.abstract: Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) are increasingly implemented as state-regulated hybrid mechanisms rather than voluntary markets, particularly in developing countries. While these schemes are often evaluated on their revenue generation, the equity implications of their non-market pricing remain under-scrutinized. This study evaluates the distributive equity of Vietnam’s national PFES program in the Northwest uplands. Integrating economic valuation with Latent Class Analysis (LCA), we identify a profound equity gap. Results indicate that state-mandated payments cover only 8.3%–16.7% of the estimated economic value of hydrological services, effectively creating a regressive subsidy from resource-constrained forest stewards to the services users. Despite this disparity, LCA reveals that the conservation burden is borne disproportionately by the poorest ethnic minority households, who sustain participation through institutional bricolage and customary norms. Conversely, the land-poor are structurally excluded by the area-based payment design. We theorize this as a hybridity trap, where the state relies on the uncompensated social capital of marginalized groups to offset policy inefficiencies. We conclude that moving from passive land rents to active labor-based benefit sharing is essential to align administrative efficiency with social justice.

title: Asymmetric Peg Dynamics in USD Stablecoins: Distributional Evidence and State-Dependent Persistence

detail.title: Asymmetric Peg Dynamics in USD Stablecoins: Distributional Evidence and State-Dependent Persistence
detail.abstract: Using daily data (2017–2025), the paper investigates peg dynamics for USDT and USDC. It shows that peg deviations are distributionally skewed and that downside departures are significantly larger and more frequent than upside ones. Negative deviations appear more persistent than positive ones and formal tests fail to reject the coefficient equality. Results also show that USDC exhibits state-dependent stability, that its persistence is negligible during tranquil periods, but it spikes to USDT-like levels during market stress (Wald  = 37.90, p < 0.001), a shift driven by stablecoin-specific rather than market-wide instability. In contrast, USDT maintains uniformly high persistence regardless of market conditions. These structural differences suggest that the two coins rely on fundamentally different stability mechanisms, posing distinct challenges for stablecoin design and regulatory oversight.

title: The Impact of GENIUS Act on Stablecoins Stability
affiliations: Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, Canadian University of Dubai and American University in Dubai

detail.title: The Impact of GENIUS Act on Stablecoins Stability
detail.abstract: The study examined the impact of the U.S. GENIUS Act passed in 2025 on dynamic dependence be- tween stablecoins and Bitcoin. The analysis centers around two key legislative milestones - Senate passage and House approval. The approach used a BEKK-GARCH framework and pre- and post-event analysis, to assess changes in conditional covariance and volatility spillovers among major centralized and decentralized stablecoins and Bitcoin. While the conditional correlations are low, the results show that the Senate passage triggered statistically significant spillover effects across all assets, indicating regulatory-induced contagion. Based on cumulative abnormal return analysis, heterogeneous responses across stablecoin types are revealed, with centralized and decentralized issuers exhibiting differing sensitivities to regulatory uncertainty. In contrast, market reactions to the subsequent House approval were weaker, suggesting that regulatory information was largely incorporated following the initial legislative approval.
